request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Age: 34
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
Patient with platin-resistant metastatic ovarian cancer was admitted to the hospital after experiencing fever and chills during infusion of nivolumab. Physical examination showed nausea and a known pelvic mass. Infusion was stopped and antihistamines and corticosteroids were administered. However, the patient remained febrile and was found to have a positive blood culture for bacillus Gram-positive bacteria. Combination therapy with antibiotics was started, but three blood cultures returned positive for rapidly growing mycobacteria. The port-a-cath was removed and antibiotics were switched to clarithromycin and ethambutol. Diagnosis of M. mucogenicum port-a-cath related bloodstream infection was retained.

Treatment and Management:
Patient received combination antibiotherapy for two months and antibiotics were pursued for six months. Despite concomitant chemotherapy, no relapse of infection was observed after antibiotic discontinuation.

Follow-up:
Patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to continue chemotherapy and to monitor for any signs of infection.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the admission was a port-a-cath related bloodstream infection caused by M. mucogenicum, a rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium.

There are two candidate codes:
- A31.- covers infection due to other mycobacteria (A31.8 other, A31.9 unspecified). This is the code for the organism.
- T80.2 covers infections following infusion, transfusion and therapeutic injection. T82.7 covers infection and inflammatory reaction due to other cardiac and vascular devices, implants and grafts, and is the usual code for catheter-related bloodstream infection with a central venous catheter.

In ICD-10-AM, a catheter-related bloodstream infection is coded to T80.2 or T82.7, depending on the device. A port-a-cath is a totally implanted vascular access device, so T82.7 applies. The organism is then added as an additional code (A31.8, with B96.- or similar).

The admission began with fever and chills during the nivolumab infusion, but the established cause after investigation was the port infection. The principal diagnosis is therefore the device-related infection.

CODE: T82
